introduction: These readings ask for contentment with what God has decreed: to hold that whatever happens has a wisdom, to give thanks in hardship, to want few things, to adapt to every circumstance, and to pray to be made content. They pair this with effort; the first of them says that peace comes 'through effort and resignation' together. A hundred of the guide's 131 quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Job's 'the Lord gave', Gethsemane, Paul content in prison, the psalms of trust, the Qur'an's comely patience, Marcus Aurelius, Dante, Milton, Julian of Norwich. Ten push back or add a side: Thoreau calls resignation confirmed desperation, Douglass and Tennyson's Ulysses refuse to yield, Job argues his case, Voltaire will not call a disaster good, Mill prefers Socrates dissatisfied, and the importunate widow, Jacob at the ford and a psalmist's 'how long?' show kinds of prayer that do not keep quiet.
questions: The first reading says that peace is found 'through effort and resignation'. In something you are facing now, what is the part of effort and what is the part of resignation?
Thoreau says that what is called resignation is confirmed desperation. How would you tell the contentment these readings describe from giving up?
Douglass says that power concedes nothing without a demand. Does contentment with God's decree mean accepting injustice done by people? Where do the readings draw that line?
Job argued with God and was told he had spoken rightly; the widow in the parable would not stop asking. Is there room inside contentment for protest and persistence?
Several readings give thanks in the middle of affliction. What makes that honest and not a pretence?
One reading counsels having few habits and being satisfied with little. What would you not miss?

outside.why: This is the verse quoted, in the Qur'an: surely We shall try you with something of fear and hunger, but give glad tidings to the steadfast.
Proverbs says that a man's heart deviseth his way, but the Lord directeth his steps.
Nehemiah, rebuilding under threat, says: we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch day and night.
Paul writes: bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Peter's letter says: humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you.
Habakkuk says that though the fig tree shall not blossom and the fields yield no meat, yet he will rejoice in the Lord.
Paul asks the Romans: if God be for us, who can be against us?
The psalmist cries: how long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? The same psalm ends in trust. Is complaint to God a failure of contentment, or one of the ways there?
At the grave of a friend Jesus wept, and those who stood by said: behold how he loved him.
The Qur'an says that it may happen that ye hate a thing which is good for you, and love a thing which is bad for you.
Paul writes that all things work together for good to them that love God.
Voltaire asked, after an earthquake had buried a city, whether a general bliss can be composed from individuals' woes. To whom, and when, can it be said that whatever occurs is good?
Isaiah has God say: my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.
Proverbs says: trust in the Lord with all thine heart, and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Paul writes from prison: rejoice in the Lord alway, and again I say, rejoice.
Paul writes that he has learned, in whatsoever state he is, therewith to be content, both to abound and to suffer need.
Paul's letter says that godliness with contentment is great gain, and that having food and raiment we should be content.
Proverbs says that better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Kipling asks whether you can meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same.
In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup be removed, and adds: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.
The Lord's Prayer asks: thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
Paul says that with him it is a very small thing that he should be judged of man's judgment.
Shakespeare's banished duke says that sweet are the uses of adversity, and finds good in every thing.
Dante's Piccarda says that it is of the essence of the blessed life to keep within the divine will.
Marcus Aurelius says to the universe: everything harmonizes with me which is harmonious to thee; nothing is too early or too late for me which is in due time for thee.
Acts tells how Paul and Silas, beaten and in prison, prayed at midnight and sang praises unto God.
The psalmist says: return unto thy rest, O my soul, for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee.
The psalm says that weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Lovelace wrote from prison that stone walls do not a prison make, for minds innocent and quiet.

Thoreau said that the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation, and that what is called resignation is confirmed desperation. How is the adaptation advised here to be told from the resignation he means?
Job says to his wife: shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?
The psalm says: O taste and see that the Lord is good; blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
Moses's blessing says: the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.
The psalm says: commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him, and he shall bring it to pass.
Paul writes: in every thing give thanks, for this is the will of God concerning you.
Pope held that all partial evil is universal good, and that whatever is, is right.

Job, in his affliction, wishes he could find God, order his cause before him, and fill his mouth with arguments; and at the end God says that Job spoke rightly. Are those who become agitated in trial only weak souls?
Paul writes about the dead, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.
James says: ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
Old Eli, told of the judgment on his house, answers: it is the Lord; let him do what seemeth him good.
James says: blessed is the man that endureth temptation, for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life.
Paul says that we glory in tribulations, for tribulation worketh patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
Ruth says to Naomi: whither thou goest, I will go, and where thou lodgest, I will lodge.
Lamentations says that it is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.
The letter to the Hebrews says: be content with such things as ye have, for he hath said, I will never leave thee.
Jesus says: take my yoke upon you, for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
The Preacher says that to every thing there is a season: a time to weep, and a time to laugh.

Hamlet finds that thinking too precisely makes cowards of us all, and enterprises of great pith and moment lose the name of action. When is bowing the head to destiny wisdom, and when the loss he describes?
Paul is told: my grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness.
Jesus says: blessed are ye when men shall revile you and persecute you; rejoice, and be exceeding glad.
Peter's letter says: think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, but rejoice.
Paul describes himself as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
Job says: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
James says: count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations, knowing that the trying of your faith worketh patience.
Paul's friends, unable to dissuade him from going to Jerusalem, ceased, saying: the will of the Lord be done.

Frederick Douglass said that if there is no struggle there is no progress, and that power concedes nothing without a demand. Does resignation to God's decree include resignation to what other people decree?
Milton, blind, concludes that those who best bear God's mild yoke serve him best: they also serve who only stand and wait.
In the Qur'an Jacob, shown his son's shirt with false blood on it, says that his course is comely patience.
In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup may pass from him: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
The psalm repeats its refrain after every memory, good and hard: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Augustine prays, his whole hope being in mercy: give what you command, and command what you will.
The Qur'an has God proclaim: if ye give thanks, I will give you more.
The psalmist tells himself: bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits.
The Song of Solomon says that many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
Jesus tells of a widow who would not stop asking an unjust judge for her right, and commends her persistence as a pattern for prayer. How does her refusal to be quiet fit with not complaining?
Paul writes: be careful for nothing, but in every thing by prayer and thanksgiving let your requests be made known.
In the Revelation Christ says: behold, I stand at the door, and knock; if any man open, I will come in and sup with him.
Jesus says: take therefore no thought for the morrow; sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
The prayer in Proverbs asks: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me.
The psalmist prays: create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.
Jesus says: let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Samuel tells the king that to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Isaiah asks: shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?
Paul says of Christ that he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death.
The psalm says that they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Jesus tells his hearers: ye are the light of the world; let your light so shine before men.
Isaiah tells his people that their iniquities have separated between them and their God.
The psalm says: he maketh me to lie down in green pastures; he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Jacob wrestles all night with one he cannot name and says: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. Is there a kind of prayer that submits by holding on?
Mary answers the angel: behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.
Marcus Aurelius says: another prays, how shall I be released from this? Pray thou: how shall I not desire to be released?
The psalm puts it in a few words: be still, and know that I am God.
Tennyson's old Ulysses will not rest, but means to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield. Is 'no recourse except to be content' the opposite of his temper, or its companion?
Isaiah says: thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.
Jesus tells his disciples, speaking of troubles to come: in your patience possess ye your souls.
Paul says that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are.
The Preacher says that better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.
Paul asks: shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, why hast thou made me thus?
Proverbs says that the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord.
Longfellow tells his sad heart to cease repining: thy fate is the common fate of all; into each life some rain must fall.
The psalmist says that he has behaved and quieted himself, as a child that is weaned of his mother.
The Qur'an says that God tasketh not a soul beyond its scope, and teaches a prayer not to be burdened beyond strength.
The psalmist says almost the same words: truly I am thy servant, and the son of thine handmaid.
Rabi'a prays that her share of this world and the next be given to others: thou art enough for me.
The psalmist asks: teach me thy way, O Lord; unite my heart to fear thy name.
The Qur'an tells the Prophet to say: I have surrendered my purpose to God.
The psalmist asks that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be acceptable.
Mill held that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. Is the one who complains always lower than the one who is content?
The psalmist says: I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope.
Julian of Norwich was shown that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.

hebrews-content-with-such-things.text: Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me

ecclesiastes-handful-with-quietness.text: Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit

peter-casting-all-your-care.text: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you

samuel-let-him-do-what-seemeth-him-good.text: And Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing from him. And he said, It is the Lord: let him do what seemeth him good

luke-importunate-widow.text: There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me

genesis-except-thou-bless-me.text: And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him. And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me
